claim: von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is a rare hereditary cancer syndrome that causes a predisposition to renal clear-cell carcinoma, hemangioblastoma, pheochromocytoma, and autosomal-recessive familial polycythemia.
source: von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is a rare hereditary cancer syndrome that causes a predisposition to renal clear-cell carcinoma, hemangioblastoma, pheochromocytoma, and autosomal-recessive familial polycythemia.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about VHL disease that draws from established scientific knowledge and consensus in the field.

claim: pVHL is the substrate conferring subunit of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex that binds to the three hypoxia-inducible factor alpha subunits (HIF1-3α) for polyubiquitylation under conditions of normoxia.
source: pVHL is the substrate conferring subunit of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex that binds to the three hypoxia-inducible factor alpha subunits (HIF1-3α) for polyubiquitylation under conditions of normoxia, targeting them for immediate degradation by the proteasome.
evidence: This describes the established molecular function of pVHL based on scientific knowledge.

claim: Certain mutations in pVHL have been determined to be causative of VHL disease through the disruption of HIFα degradation.
source: Certain mutations in pVHL have been determined to be causative of VHL disease through the disruption of HIFα degradation.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about the mechanism of VHL disease.

claim: VHL disease afflicts approximately 1 in 35,000 people.
source: VHL disease is rare, afflicting approximately 1 in 35,000 people (Neumann and Wiestler, 1991; Maher et al., 1991).
evidence: This epidemiological claim is supported by citations to Neumann and Wiestler, 1991 and Maher et al., 1991.

claim: VHL disease includes cardinal features of retinal and central nervous system hemangioblastoma, clear-cell renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic, renal and epididymal cysts, endolymphatic sac tumors, and polycythemia.
source: In addition to the retinal and central nervous system hemangioblastoma, other cardinal features of VHL disease include clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC), the commonest form of kidney cancer, and pheochromocytoma, a neuroendocrine tumor derived from adrenal chromaffin cells, in addition to pancreatic, renal and epididymal cysts, endolymphatic sac tumors, and polycythemia (Lindau, 1904 ; Davison et al., 1936; Hippel, 1904).
evidence: This clinical description is supported by historical citations to Lindau, 1904; Davison et al., 1936; and Hippel, 1904.

claim: The VHL gene was cloned in 1993 and mutations of the locus were determined to be causative of VHL disease.
source: In 1993, the VHL gene was cloned and mutations of the locus were determined to be causative of VHL disease (Latif et al., 1993).
evidence: This historical claim is supported by citation to Latif et al., 1993.

claim: VHL disease is broadly separated into two types based on the propensity of developing pheochromocytoma where Type 1 patients have a low risk while Type 2 patients have a high risk of pheochromocytoma.
source: First, VHL disease is broadly separated into two types based on the propensity of developing pheochromocytoma where Type 1 patients have a low risk while Type 2 patients have a high risk of pheochromocytoma.
evidence: This is a classification statement based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: Type 1 VHL disease patients develop hemangioblastoma and RCC.
source: Type 1 patients also develop hemangioblastoma and RCC.
evidence: This is a clinical characterization based on established knowledge.

claim: Type 2 VHL disease is stratified into Type 2a (high risk of hemangioblastoma with low risk of RCC), Type 2b (high risk of hemangioblastoma and RCC), and Type 2c (only pheochromocytoma without the other disease manifestations).
source: Type 2 disease is further stratified into Type 2a (high risk of hemangioblastoma with low risk of RCC), Type 2b (high risk of hemangioblastoma and RCC), and Type 2c (only pheochromocytoma without the other disease manifestations).
evidence: This is a classification statement based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: VHL mutations have been found to be causative of autosomal-recessive familial polycythemia, which is sometimes referred to as Type 3 VHL disease.
source: Moreover, VHL mutations have been found to be causative of autosomal-recessive familial polycythemia, which is sometimes referred to as Type 3 VHL disease (Table 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Table 1 which shows the classification.

claim: VHL disease Type 1 and 2 are inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner.
source: VHL disease Type 1 and 2 are inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner, which predisposes an individual to developing cancer upon the loss of the remaining wild-type allele.
evidence: This describes the inheritance pattern based on established genetic knowledge.

claim: Loss of heterozygosity resulting from large deletions, mitotic recombination, or hypermethylation of the wild-type allele in a susceptible cell is required for a tumor to form in VHL disease Type 1 and 2.
source: In other words, there must be a loss of heterozygosity resulting either from large deletions, mitotic recombination, or hypermethylation of the wild-type allele in a susceptible cell for a tumor to form (Prowse et al., 1997).
evidence: This mechanistic claim is supported by citation to Prowse et al., 1997.

claim: To develop polycythemia associated with VHL disease Type 3, an individual must inherit two mutated VHL alleles, meaning it is an autosomal-recessive disease.
source: However, to develop polycythemia associated with VHL disease Type 3, an individual must inherit two mutated VHL alleles, meaning it is an autosomal-recessive disease.
evidence: This describes the inheritance pattern based on established genetic knowledge.

claim: pVHL forms an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex with elongin B, elongin C, cullin 2, and Rbx1.
source: The protein product of VHL is termed pVHL, which forms an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex (pVHL-E3) with elongin B, elongin C, cullin 2, and Rbx1 (Kamura et al., 1999; Cardote et al., 2017).
evidence: This molecular composition claim is supported by citations to Kamura et al., 1999 and Cardote et al., 2017.

claim: pVHL serves as the substrate-conferring component of the pVHL-E3 ligase, an integral component in the metazoan oxygen-sensing pathway.
source: pVHL serves as the substrate-conferring component of the pVHL-E3 ligase, an integral component in the metazoan oxygen-sensing pathway (Figure 1).
evidence: This functional description is supported by reference to Figure 1 and reflects established knowledge.

claim: The best-characterized substrates of the pVHL-E3 ligase are the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) alpha subunit paralogs HIF1α, HIF2α, and HIF3α.
source: The best-characterized substrates of the pVHL-E3 ligase remain the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) alpha subunit paralogs HIF1α, HIF2α, and HIF3α.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about pVHL substrates.

claim: HIFs are heterodimeric transcription factors consisting of an oxygen-labile α subunit and a constitutively expressed β subunit.
source: HIFs are heterodimeric transcription factors consisting of an oxygen-labile α subunit and a constitutively expressed β subunit (Figure 1).
evidence: This structural description is supported by Figure 1 and reflects established knowledge.

claim: In the presence of sufficient oxygen, prolyl hydroxylase (PHD) enzymes hydroxylate the conserved proline residues on HIFα, which results in pVHL binding to HIFα and subsequent polyubiquitylation leading to 26 S proteasomal-mediated degradation of HIFα.
source: In the presence of sufficient oxygen, prolyl hydroxylase (PHD) enzymes hydroxylate the conserved proline residues on HIFα, which results in pVHL binding to HIFα and subsequent polyubiquitylation leading to 26 S proteasomal-mediated degradation of HIFα (Figure 1; Epstein et al., 2001; Jaakkola et al., 2001; Ivan et al., 2001; Bruick and McKnight, 2001).
evidence: This mechanistic claim is supported by Figure 1 and multiple citations: Epstein et al., 2001; Jaakkola et al., 2001; Ivan et al., 2001; Bruick and McKnight, 2001.

claim: Under hypoxic conditions, HIFα remains unhydroxylated, escapes recognition via pVHL, and is therefore not degraded.
source: Under hypoxic conditions, HIFα remains unhydroxylated, escapes recognition via pVHL, and is therefore not degraded.
evidence: This mechanistic description reflects established knowledge about the oxygen-sensing pathway.

claim: Stabilized HIFα is able to dimerize with HIFβ and translocate to the nucleus where it transcriptionally regulates many genes involved in the adaptive hypoxic response including metabolic enzymes, erythropoietin (EPO), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).
source: This pool of stabilized HIFα is able to both dimerize with HIFβ and translocate to the nucleus where it transcriptionally regulates many genes involved in the adaptive hypoxic response including metabolic enzymes, erythropoietin (EPO), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) (Figure 1; Jiang et al., 1996).
evidence: This functional description is supported by Figure 1 and citation to Jiang et al., 1996.

claim: Several Type 2c pVHL mutants were found to promote HIFα polyubiquitylation at seemingly wild-type levels.
source: Type 2c VHL disease is associated with pheochromocytoma without other disease phenotypes, and several Type 2c pVHL mutants were found to promote HIFα polyubiquitylation at seemingly wild-type levels (Hoffman et al., 2001; Clifford et al., 2001).
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citations to Hoffman et al., 2001 and Clifford et al., 2001.

claim: Type 1 VHL disease patients with mutations predicted to profoundly inactivate pVHL, including nonsense, frameshift and splicing mutations, do not develop pheochromocytoma.
source: Despite Type 1 disease driven by mutations predicted to profoundly inactivate pVHL, including nonsense, frameshift and splicing mutations, these patients do not develop pheochromocytoma (Stebbins et al., 1999; Chen et al., 1995; Crossey et al., 1995; Stolle et al., 1998).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to Stebbins et al., 1999; Chen et al., 1995; Crossey et al., 1995; Stolle et al., 1998.

claim: pVHL has been linked to the regulation of extracellular matrix proteins collagen and fibronectin.
source: Notably, pVHL has been linked to the regulation of extracellular matrix proteins collagen and fibronectin (Ohh et al., 1998; Kurban et al., 1998a; Grosfeld et al., 2007; Stickle et al., 2004; Kurban et al., 1998b)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Ohh et al., 1998; Kurban et al., 1998a; Grosfeld et al., 2007; Stickle et al., 2004; Kurban et al., 1998b.

claim: pVHL has been linked to the regulation of microtubules.
source: Notably, pVHL has been linked to the regulation of extracellular matrix proteins collagen and fibronectin (Ohh et al., 1998; Kurban et al., 1998a; Grosfeld et al., 2007; Stickle et al., 2004; Kurban et al., 1998b), microtubules (Thoma et al., 2009; Hergovich et al., 2006; Hergovich et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thoma et al., 2009; Hergovich et al., 2006; Hergovich et al., 2003.

claim: pVHL has been linked to the regulation of primary cilia.
source: Notably, pVHL has been linked to the regulation of extracellular matrix proteins collagen and fibronectin (Ohh et al., 1998; Kurban et al., 1998a; Grosfeld et al., 2007; Stickle et al., 2004; Kurban et al., 1998b), microtubules (Thoma et al., 2009; Hergovich et al., 2006; Hergovich et al., 2003), primary cilia (Montani et al., 2010; Esteban et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Montani et al., 2010 and Esteban et al., 2006.

claim: pVHL has been linked to the regulation of NFκB.
source: Notably, pVHL has been linked to the regulation of extracellular matrix proteins collagen and fibronectin (Ohh et al., 1998; Kurban et al., 1998a; Grosfeld et al., 2007; Stickle et al., 2004; Kurban et al., 1998b), microtubules (Thoma et al., 2009; Hergovich et al., 2006; Hergovich et al., 2003), primary cilia (Montani et al., 2010; Esteban et al., 2006), NFκB (Cummins et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cummins et al., 2006 and Yang et al., 2007.

claim: pVHL has been linked to the regulation of Human Antigen R (HuR).
source: Notably, pVHL has been linked to the regulation of extracellular matrix proteins collagen and fibronectin (Ohh et al., 1998; Kurban et al., 1998a; Grosfeld et al., 2007; Stickle et al., 2004; Kurban et al., 1998b), microtubules (Thoma et al., 2009; Hergovich et al., 2006; Hergovich et al., 2003), primary cilia (Montani et al., 2010; Esteban et al., 2006), NFκB (Cummins et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2007), Human Antigen R (HuR) (Danilin et al., 2009; Massfelder et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Danilin et al., 2009 and Massfelder et al., 2004.

claim: pVHL has been linked to the regulation of AKT kinase.
source: Notably, pVHL has been linked to the regulation of extracellular matrix proteins collagen and fibronectin (Ohh et al., 1998; Kurban et al., 1998a; Grosfeld et al., 2007; Stickle et al., 2004; Kurban et al., 1998b), microtubules (Thoma et al., 2009; Hergovich et al., 2006; Hergovich et al., 2003), primary cilia (Montani et al., 2010; Esteban et al., 2006), NFκB (Cummins et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2007), Human Antigen R (HuR) (Danilin et al., 2009; Massfelder et al., 2004), AKT kinase (Guo et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2016.

claim: pVHL has been linked to the regulation of p14/ARF.
source: Notably, pVHL has been linked to the regulation of extracellular matrix proteins collagen and fibronectin (Ohh et al., 1998; Kurban et al., 1998a; Grosfeld et al., 2007; Stickle et al., 2004; Kurban et al., 1998b), microtubules (Thoma et al., 2009; Hergovich et al., 2006; Hergovich et al., 2003), primary cilia (Montani et al., 2010; Esteban et al., 2006), NFκB (Cummins et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2007), Human Antigen R (HuR) (Danilin et al., 2009; Massfelder et al., 2004), AKT kinase (Guo et al., 2016), p14/ARF (Minervini et al., 2015; Lai et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Minervini et al., 2015 and Lai et al., 2011.

claim: pVHL has been linked to the regulation of ZHX2.
source: Notably, pVHL has been linked to the regulation of extracellular matrix proteins collagen and fibronectin (Ohh et al., 1998; Kurban et al., 1998a; Grosfeld et al., 2007; Stickle et al., 2004; Kurban et al., 1998b), microtubules (Thoma et al., 2009; Hergovich et al., 2006; Hergovich et al., 2003), primary cilia (Montani et al., 2010; Esteban et al., 2006), NFκB (Cummins et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2007), Human Antigen R (HuR) (Danilin et al., 2009; Massfelder et al., 2004), AKT kinase (Guo et al., 2016), p14/ARF (Minervini et al., 2015; Lai et al., 2011), and ZHX2 (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: A systemic attempt to detect PHD-mediated hydroxylation of 24 non-HIFα substrates failed to reproduce and confirm previously published findings.
source: Notably, a systemic attempt to detect PHD-mediated hydroxylation of 24 non-HIFα substrates failed to reproduce and confirm previously published findings (Cockman et al., 2019).
evidence: This negative result is supported by citation to Cockman et al., 2019.

claim: Fibronectin, collagen, tubulin, HuR, and p14/ARF have been identified as pVHL interactors in high throughput studies with additional low-throughput supporting evidence in the BioGRID database.
source: Further, a list of potential pVHL substrates, including fibronectin, collagen, tubulin, HuR, and p14/ARF, have been identified as pVHL interactors in high throughput studies with additional low-throughput supporting evidence in the BioGRID database (Oughtred et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the BioGRID database (Oughtred et al., 2021).

claim: Each of the potential pVHL interactors (fibronectin, collagen, tubulin, HuR, and p14/ARF) have only been identified in a single high-throughput experiment and all but HuR have been identified by the same high-throughput study.
source: Each of these potential interactors, however, have only been identified in a single high-throughput experiment and all but HuR have been identified by the same high-throughput study (Lai et al., 2011; Oughtred et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lai et al., 2011 and Oughtred et al., 2021.

claim: The HIFα substrates of pVHL have been identified by numerous high-throughput and low throughput studies (143 identify HIF1α and 19 identify HIF2α in the BioGRID database).
source: In contrast, the HIFα substrates of pVHL have been identified by numerous high-throughput and low throughput studies (143 identify HIF1α and 19 identify HIF2α in the BioGRID database) demonstrating a disparity in the confidence of the interactions (Oughtred et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the BioGRID database (Oughtred et al., 2021) with specific numbers provided.

claim: Patients with large deletion and frameshift mutations generally develop Type 1 VHL disease, while patients with missense mutations develop Type 2 disease.
source: Patients with large deletion and frameshift mutations generally develop Type 1 VHL disease, while patients with missense mutations develop Type 2 disease (Chen et al., 1995; Stolle et al., 1998; Maher et al., 1996).
evidence: This genotype-phenotype correlation is supported by citations to Chen et al., 1995; Stolle et al., 1998; Maher et al., 1996.

claim: Type 2c pVHL mutants cause exclusively pheochromocytoma and have been shown to degrade HIFα nearly as well as wild-type pVHL.
source: Type 2c pVHL mutants, for example, cause exclusively pheochromocytoma and have been shown to degrade HIFα nearly as well as wild-type pVHL (Hoffman et al., 2001).
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citation to Hoffman et al., 2001.

claim: The various clinical phenotypes associated with VHL disease require different 'doses' of HIF.
source: Thus, we propose that the various clinical phenotypes associated with VHL disease require different 'doses' of HIF.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on inference from clinical observations.

claim: From polycythemia to pheochromocytoma to hemangioma/hemangioblastoma to RCC, a greater dose of HIF is required for disease onset.
source: From polycythemia to pheochromocytoma to hemangioma/hemangioblastoma to RCC, a greater dose of HIF is required for disease onset.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on inference from clinical observations.

claim: The Y98H VHL mutation appears to result in hemangioma/hemangioblastoma in approximately 50% of cases while the Y112H mutation displays hemangioma/hemangioblastoma in only 20% of cases.
source: Both the Y98H and Y112H VHL mutations are classically associated with VHL Type 2a disease with a high penetrance of pheochromocytoma, but while the Y112H mutation appears to result in hemangioma/hemangioblastoma in only 20% of cases, the Y98H mutation displays a greater penetrance at ~50% (Brauch et al., 1995; Chen et al., 1996).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to Brauch et al., 1995 and Chen et al., 1996.

claim: Patients with the Y98H pVHL mutation are diagnosed earlier (mean of 19.7 years-old) than patients with the Y112H pVHL mutation (28.8 years-old).
source: This observation is also consistent with the fact that patients with the Y98H pVHL mutation are diagnosed earlier (mean of 19.7 years-old) than patients with the Y112H pVHL mutation (28.8 years-old) (Nielsen et al., 2011a).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citation to Nielsen et al., 2011a.

claim: In a study of 16 families harboring the Y98H mutation, out of 116 affected family members, 73 developed pheochromocytoma while 4 developed RCC.
source: A study of 16 families harboring the Y98H mutation found that some affected individuals exhibited symptoms consistent with Type 1 or 2b VHL disease. Out of 116 affected family members, 73 developed pheochromocytoma while 4 developed RCC (Brauch et al., 1995).
evidence: This clinical data is supported by citation to Brauch et al., 1995.

claim: Approximately 3% of individuals with the Y112H mutations also develop RCC.
source: Similarly, ~3% of individuals with the Y112H mutations also develop RCC (Nielsen et al., 2011b).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citation to Nielsen et al., 2011b.

claim: In a family harboring Y112N, 7 individuals developed RCC and only one developed pheochromocytoma, suggesting Y112N presents more commonly as Type 1 VHL disease.
source: In comparison, in a family harboring Y112N, 7 individuals developed RCC and only one developed pheochromocytoma, suggesting Y112N presents more commonly as Type 1 VHL disease (Bradley et al., 1999).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citation to Bradley et al., 1999.

claim: The Type 2c VHL mutant V84L is associated solely with pheochromocytoma in most patients but in some cases, vascular tumors, including the possibility of spinal hemangioblastoma, and renal cysts are observed.
source: One example is the classic Type 2c VHL mutant V84L, which is associated solely with pheochromocytoma in most patients but in some cases, vascular tumors, including the possibility of spinal hemangioblastoma, and renal cysts are observed (Abbott et al., 2006).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citation to Abbott et al., 2006.

claim: The Type 2c VHL mutant G93S was linked with pheochromocytoma across multiple generations in a family with VHL disease, but further diagnostic workup revealed two retinal angiomas in the index patient and bilateral renal cysts in the index patient's father.
source: Similarly, the Type 2c VHL mutant G93S was linked with pheochromocytoma across multiple generations in a family with VHL disease, but further diagnostic workup revealed two retinal angiomas in the index patient and bilateral renal cysts in the index patient's father (Schreinemakers et al., 2007).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citation to Schreinemakers et al., 2007.

claim: A patient with bilateral pheochromocytoma and no other VHL-related symptoms was found to harbor a Y175C VHL mutation.
source: For example, a patient with bilateral pheochromocytoma and no other VHL-related symptoms was found to harbor a Y175C VHL mutation.
evidence: This is a clinical case description.

claim: Y175C pVHL was able to degrade HIF efficiently under normoxic conditions when compared to wild-type pVHL.
source: When compared to wild-type pVHL, Y175C pVHL was able to degrade HIF efficiently under normoxic conditions (Astapova et al., 2018).
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citation to Astapova et al., 2018.

claim: Pheochromocytoma carcinogenesis is clinically associated with PHD2 loss-of-function mutations and HIF2α gain-of-function mutations in addition to pVHL loss-of-function mutations.
source: Of particular interest, pheochromocytoma carcinogenesis is clinically associated with PHD2 loss-of-function mutations and HIF2α gain-of-function mutations in addition to pVHL loss-of-function mutations (Gardie et al., 2014; Ladroue et al., 2008; Därr et al., 2016; Taieb et al., 2016; Tarade et al., 2018).
evidence: This clinical association is supported by citations to Gardie et al., 2014; Ladroue et al., 2008; Därr et al., 2016; Taieb et al., 2016; Tarade et al., 2018.

claim: Patients with mutations in EPAS1, the gene encoding HIF2α, have been reported to develop polycythemia and neuroendocrine tumors in dozens of patients.
source: Patients with mutations in EPAS1, the gene encoding HIF2α, have been reported to develop polycythemia and neuroendocrine tumors in dozens of patients (Därr et al., 2016; Taieb et al., 2016; Tarade et al., 2018).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to Därr et al., 2016; Taieb et al., 2016; Tarade et al., 2018.

claim: HIF2-driven disease can be segregated into two broad classes: Class 1 characterized by the presence of pheochromocytoma and/or paraganglioma (PPGL) with or without polycythemia, and Class 2 in which patients present solely with polycythemia.
source: HIF2-driven disease can be segregated into two broad classes: Class 1 characterized by the presence of pheochromocytoma and/or paraganglioma (PPGL) with or without polycythemia, and Class 2 in which patients present solely with polycythemia (Tarade et al., 2018).
evidence: This classification is supported by citation to Tarade et al., 2018.

claim: Class 1 HIF2-driven disease is further divided into three sub-classes where Class 1a presents with PPGL, somatostatinoma, and polycythemia, Class 1b presents with PPGL and polycythemia, and Class 1c presents with PPGL exclusively.
source: Class 1 is further divided into three sub-classes where Class 1a presents with PPGL, somatostatinoma, and polycythemia, Class 1b presents with PPGL and polycythemia, and Class 1c presents with PPGL exclusively (Table 2).
evidence: This classification is supported by reference to Table 2.

claim: There is a single case of hemangioblastoma linked to a HIF2α gain-of-function mutation, a unique and uncharacterized double F374Y and Q561K missense mutation.
source: While there is only a single case of hemangioblastoma linked to a HIF2α gain-of-function mutation, a unique and uncharacterized double F374Y and Q561K missense mutation, (Taieb et al., 2016)
evidence: This clinical case is supported by citation to Taieb et al., 2016.

claim: The clinical literature includes three reports of patients with HIF2-driven disease developing hemangiomas of the retina, liver, and cranial vault.
source: the clinical literature includes three reports of patients with HIF2-driven disease developing hemangiomas of the retina, liver, and cranial vault (Pacak et al., 2013; Dmitriev et al., 2020; Buffet et al., 2014).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to Pacak et al., 2013; Dmitriev et al., 2020; Buffet et al., 2014.

claim: Liver hemangiomas associated with loss-of-pVHL mouse models can be rescued by co-deletion of HIF2α or HIFβ.
source: While there is less clinical evidence of HIF2α driving hemangioma, relative to PPGL, liver hemangiomas associated with loss-of-pVHL mouse models can be rescued by co-deletion of HIF2α or HIFβ, which provides further evidence for the gatekeeping role of HIF2α in hemangioma and hemangioblastoma (Rankin et al., 2008; Rankin et al., 2005).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citations to Rankin et al., 2008 and Rankin et al., 2005.

claim: PHD2 mutations have been widely found to cause polycythemia.
source: PHD2 mutations have been widely found to cause polycythemia.
evidence: This is a statement of established clinical knowledge.

claim: PHD2 mutations, like PHD2 H374R and PHD2 A228S, trigger development of pheochromocytoma and/or paraganglioma (PPGL) in addition to polycythemia.
source: More rarely, PHD2 mutations, like PHD2 H374R and PHD2 A228S, trigger development of pheochromocytoma and/or paraganglioma (PPGL) in addition to polycythemia (Gardie et al., 2014; Ladroue et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to Gardie et al., 2014; Ladroue et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2015.

claim: The patient harboring the H374R PHD2 mutant originally presented with erythrocytosis, but a tumor matching the characteristics of a paraganglioma was later diagnosed at 43 years old.
source: The patient harboring the H374R mutant originally presented with erythrocytosis, but a tumor matching the characteristics of a paraganglioma was later diagnosis at 43 years old (Ladroue et al., 2008)
evidence: This clinical case is supported by citation to Ladroue et al., 2008.

claim: The patient with H374R PHD2 mutation displayed loss of the remaining wild-type EGLN1 allele.
source: This individual displayed loss of the remaining wild-type EGLN1 allele.
evidence: This is a genetic observation from the clinical case.

claim: Deletion of a single PHD2 allele or knock-in of a single mutant PHD2 allele in mice successfully recapitulates polycythemia, which was also found to be dependent on HIF2α.
source: Indeed, deletion of a single PHD2 allele or knock-in of a single mutant PHD2 allele in mice successfully recapitulates polycythemia, which was also found to be dependent on HIF2α (Arsenault et al., 2013).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citation to Arsenault et al., 2013.

claim: There has been one documented case of a disease-causing PHD1 mutation, S61R, which induced erythrocytosis development by age 6 and recurrent PPGL at age 14.
source: Indeed, there has been one documented case of a disease-causing PHD1 mutation. This mutant, S61R, induced erythrocytosis development by age 6 and recurrent PPGL at age 14 (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This clinical case is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: R200W and H191D have both been identified as autosomal-recessive pVHL mutations that cause polycythemia.
source: There have also been documented cases of pVHL mutant-induced polycythemia (Type 3 VHL disease). R200W and H191D have both been identified as autosomal-recessive pVHL mutations that cause polycythemia (Pastore et al., 2003; Ang et al., 2002).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to Pastore et al., 2003 and Ang et al., 2002.

claim: Inhibition of HIF2α rescues polycythemia in mouse models of polycythemia driven by the R200W mutation.
source: And similarly to the role of HIF2α in liver hemangioma pathogenesis in loss-of-pVHL mouse models, inhibition of HIF2α rescues polycythemia in mouse models of polycythemia driven by the R200W mutation (Ghosh et al., 2021; Hickey et al., 2007; Ghosh et al., 2018).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2021; Hickey et al., 2007; Ghosh et al., 2018.

claim: A study investigating eight children with polycythemia revealed one case in which a family harbored a heterozygous VHL mutant (D126Y) inducing a phenotype.
source: While pVHL induced polycythemia is generally inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner, a study investigating eight children with polycythemia revealed one case in which a family harbored a heterozygous VHL mutant inducing a phenotype. Two siblings in the family were found to be heterozygous for D126Y and had increased levels of hematocrit and erythropoietin.
evidence: This is a clinical case description.

claim: Two siblings heterozygous for D126Y VHL mutation had increased levels of hematocrit and erythropoietin.
source: Two siblings in the family were found to be heterozygous for D126Y and had increased levels of hematocrit and erythropoietin.
evidence: This is a clinical observation.

claim: One of the siblings with D126Y VHL mutation had a history of tumors, developing a pulmonary angioma at age 10 and a renal subcapsular hemangioma at age 15.
source: One of the siblings had a history of tumors, developing a pulmonary angioma at age 10 and a renal subcapsular hemangioma at age 15.
evidence: This is a clinical case description.

claim: All the patients in the polycythemia study were young (10–19 years old).
source: All the patients in this study were young (10–19 years old; Pastore et al., 2003)
evidence: This demographic information is supported by citation to Pastore et al., 2003.

claim: The oxygen-sensing pathway in humans is canonically comprised of three PHD paralogs (PHD1, PHD2, PHD3), three HIFα paralogs (HIF1α, HIF2α, HIF3α), two HIFβ paralogs (ARNT and ARNT2), and a single pVHL-E3 ligase.
source: The oxygen-sensing pathway in humans is canonically comprised of three PHD paralogs (PHD1, PHD2, PHD3), three HIFα paralogs (HIF1α, HIF2α, HIF3α), two HIFβ paralogs (ARNT and ARNT2), and a single pVHL-E3 ligase (Figure 1; Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008).
evidence: This description of the pathway is supported by Figure 1 and citation to Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008.

claim: Each PHD paralog has varying hydroxylation activity toward the HIFα paralogs.
source: The complexity of the pathway is also influenced by the differential behavior of the paralogs of each component; each PHD paralog has varying hydroxylation activity toward the HIFα paralogs (Appelhoff et al., 2004)
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citation to Appelhoff et al., 2004.

claim: Each HIFα paralog has 2 hydroxylation sites with varying oxygen-dependent hydroxylation sensitivities.
source: The complexity of the pathway is also influenced by the differential behavior of the paralogs of each component; each PHD paralog has varying hydroxylation activity toward the HIFα paralogs (Appelhoff et al., 2004), each HIFα paralog has 2 hydroxylation sites with varying oxygen-dependent hydroxylation sensitivities (Tarhonskaya et al., 2015)
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citation to Tarhonskaya et al., 2015.

claim: HIF3α has multiple splice variants.
source: The complexity of the pathway is also influenced by the differential behavior of the paralogs of each component; each PHD paralog has varying hydroxylation activity toward the HIFα paralogs (Appelhoff et al., 2004), each HIFα paralog has 2 hydroxylation sites with varying oxygen-dependent hydroxylation sensitivities (Tarhonskaya et al., 2015), HIF3α has multiple splice variants (Maynard et al., 2003)
evidence: This molecular observation is supported by citation to Maynard et al., 2003.

claim: The HIFα paralogs regulate partially overlapping as well as unique sets of genes.
source: The complexity of the pathway is also influenced by the differential behavior of the paralogs of each component; each PHD paralog has varying hydroxylation activity toward the HIFα paralogs (Appelhoff et al., 2004), each HIFα paralog has 2 hydroxylation sites with varying oxygen-dependent hydroxylation sensitivities (Tarhonskaya et al., 2015), HIF3α has multiple splice variants (Maynard et al., 2003) and the HIFα paralogs regulate partially overlapping as well as unique sets of genes (Schödel et al., 2011).
evidence: This functional observation is supported by citation to Schödel et al., 2011.

claim: VHL Type 1 mutations in which pVHL is grossly or completely inactivated through truncation or frameshift result in maximal stabilization of HIFα.
source: However, the degree to which the HIFα substrates are stabilized varies between the different types of mutations (Rechsteiner et al., 2011), VHL Type 1 mutations in which pVHL is grossly or completely inactivated through truncation or frameshift result in maximal stabilization of HIFα
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citation to Rechsteiner et al., 2011.

claim: VHL Type 2 mutations affecting the folding, stability, or substrate-binding interface of pVHL have an intermediate effect on HIFα stabilization due to the remaining pVHL activity.
source: whereas VHL Type 2 mutations affecting the folding, stability, or substrate-binding interface of pVHL have an intermediate effect on HIFα stabilization due to the remaining pVHL activity (Rechsteiner et al., 2011; Knauth et al., 2006; Hacker et al., 2008; Forman et al., 2009).
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citations to Rechsteiner et al., 2011; Knauth et al., 2006; Hacker et al., 2008; Forman et al., 2009.

claim: Multiple biochemical studies demonstrate that Type 2b mutations result in greater HIF stabilization than Type 2a mutations.
source: Among the various sub-types of VHL disease, multiple biochemical studies demonstrate that Type 2b mutations result in greater HIF stabilization than Type 2a mutations (Knauth et al., 2009; Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citations to Knauth et al., 2009 and Li et al., 2007.

claim: Some studies argue that Type 2c mutations result in an unstable pVHL-E3 ubiquitin ligase complex and a mild stabilization of HIF1α.
source: While multiple studies suggest that VHL Type 2c mutations do not negatively impact the ability to regulate HIFα, other studies argue that Type 2c mutations result in an unstable pVHL-E3 ubiquitin ligase complex and a mild stabilization of HIF1α (Knauth et al., 2009).
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citation to Knauth et al., 2009.

claim: Numerous missense mutations in the C-terminal prolyl-hydroxylation site in the oxygen-dependent degradation domain of HIF2α have been reported to cause polycythemia, pheochromocytoma, paraganglioma, somatostatinoma, hemangioma, and in one case hemangioblastoma.
source: Numerous missense mutations in the C-terminal prolyl-hydroxylation site in the oxygen-dependent degradation domain of HIF2α have been reported to cause polycythemia, pheochromocytoma, paraganglioma, somatostatinoma, hemangioma, and in one case hemangioblastoma (Taieb et al., 2016; Tarade et al., 2018).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to Taieb et al., 2016 and Tarade et al., 2018.

claim: The HIF2-driven disease classes are linked to unique sets of HIF2α mutations defining a genotype-phenotype correlation similar to VHL disease.
source: Notably, the HIF2-driven disease classes are linked to unique sets of HIF2α mutations defining a genotype-phenotype correlation similar to VHL disease (Tarade et al., 2018).
evidence: This genotype-phenotype correlation is supported by citation to Tarade et al., 2018.

claim: HIF2α mutations reduce the affinity of hydroxylated HIF2α to pVHL with increasing reductions in binding affinity correlated to increasing severity of the disease phenotype with Class 1 mutations being more deleterious than Class 2 mutations.
source: These HIF2α mutations reduce the affinity of hydroxylated HIF2α to pVHL with increasing reductions in binding affinity correlated to increasing severity of the disease phenotype with Class 1 mutations being more deleterious than Class 2 mutations (Tarade et al., 2018).
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citation to Tarade et al., 2018.

claim: PHD2 mutants have an impaired ability to reduce HIF1α and HIF2α levels when transfected and expressed in mammalian cells.
source: Studies have shown that PHD2 mutants have an impaired ability to reduce HIF1α and HIF2α levels when transfected and expressed in mammalian cells (Yang et al., 2015; Percy et al., 2006; Ladroue et al., 2012).
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2015; Percy et al., 2006; Ladroue et al., 2012.

claim: The PPGL-associated H374R PHD2 mutation was found to severely abrogate the capacity for HIF2α regulation relative to most mutations that cause only polycythemia.
source: Further, the PPGL-associated H374R PHD2 mutation was found to severely abrogate the capacity for HIF2α regulation relative to most mutations that cause only polycythemia (Ladroue et al., 2012).
evidence: This biochemical observation is supported by citation to Ladroue et al., 2012.

claim: Mutations in HIF2α and PHD2 have not been observed to be causative of RCC.
source: However, mutations in HIF2ɑ and PHD2 have not been observed to be causative of RCC indicating that HIF2α stabilization independent of improper HIF1α regulation is not sufficient to drive the development of RCC.
evidence: This is an observation about the absence of clinical findings.

claim: Loss-of-function PHD2 mutations or gain-of-function HIF2α mutations have not been observed in RCC.
source: Unlike the other cardinal stigmata associated with VHL disease, loss-of-function PHD2 mutations or gain-of-function HIF2α mutations have not been observed in RCC (Morris et al., 2009; Astuti et al., 2011).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to Morris et al., 2009 and Astuti et al., 2011.

claim: Human RCC 786-O cell line lacks both pVHL and HIF1α while overproducing HIF2α.
source: Human RCC 786-O cell line lacks both pVHL and HIF1α while overproducing HIF2α, making them useful for studying VHL disease.
evidence: This is a description of a cell line based on established knowledge.

claim: 786-O cells transfected with HIF2α P405A/P531A double mutants (unable to be hydroxylated by PHDs) can induce tumors in nude mice when implanted.
source: 786-O cells transfected with HIF2α P405A/P531A double mutants (unable to be hydroxylated by PHDs) can induce tumors in nude mice when implanted.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Growth of tumors from 786-O cells with HIF2α P405A/P531A double mutants can be reduced via siRNA-mediated knockdown of HIF2α, but this defect cannot be rescued by expression of a basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) HIF2α mutant incapable of DNA binding.
source: Growth of these tumors can be reduced via siRNA-mediated knockdown of HIF2α, but this defect cannot be rescued by expression of a basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) HIF2α mutant incapable of DNA binding (Kondo et al., 2003; Kondo et al., 2002; Zimmer et al., 2004).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citations to Kondo et al., 2003; Kondo et al., 2002; Zimmer et al., 2004.

claim: Loss of chromosome 14q, harboring the HIF1α gene, is a hallmark of RCC metastasis and results in poor prognosis for patients.
source: There is also evidence that the loss of chromosome 14q, harboring the HIF1α gene, is a hallmark of RCC metastasis and results in poor prognosis for patients (Shen et al., 2011; Monzon et al., 2011; Turajlic et al., 2018).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to Shen et al., 2011; Monzon et al., 2011; Turajlic et al., 2018.

claim: Downregulation of HIF1α in kidney cancer cells promotes tumor growth, while supplementing HIF1α deficient cell lines with HIF1α leads to tumor regression.
source: In addition, downregulation of HIF1α in kidney cancer cells promotes tumor growth, while supplementing HIF1α deficient cell lines with HIF1α leads to tumor regression (Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citation to Shen et al., 2011.

claim: Through the inactivation of pVHL via conditional knockout in collecting ducts and distal tubules, mice develop overt carcinoma.
source: Through the inactivation of pVHL via conditional knockout in collecting ducts and distal tubules, mice develop overt carcinoma (Pritchett et al., 2015).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citation to Pritchett et al., 2015.

claim: Deletion of HIF1α but not HIF2α completely abolishes tumorigenesis in pVHL conditional knockout mouse models.
source: Deletion of HIF1α but not HIF2α completely abolishes tumorigenesis in these models (Pritchett et al., 2015).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citation to Pritchett et al., 2015.

claim: The forced expression of HIF1α leads to the formation of dysplasia, cysts, and precancerous lesions while HIF2α expression results in only minor cellular phenotypes.
source: Further, the forced expression of HIF1α leads to the formation of dysplasia, cysts, and precancerous lesions while HIF2α expression results in only minor cellular phenotypes (Fu et al., 2011; Fu et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2013).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2011; Fu et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2013.

claim: Common mutations in tumor suppressor PBRM1 have been linked to the amplification of HIF1α signaling.
source: Further, common mutations in other tumor suppressors, such as SWI/SNF protein PBRM1, have been linked to the amplification of HIF1α signaling (Nargund et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to Nargund et al., 2017 and Gao et al., 2017.

claim: HIF1α and carbonic anhydrase IX (CAIX) staining is prominent in precancerous lesions and cysts while HIF2α is expressed most in overt carcinoma.
source: This model is further supported by the staining of human tissues, where HIF1α and carbonic anhydrase IX (CAIX) staining is prominent in precancerous lesions and cysts while HIF2α is expressed most in overt carcinoma (Mandriota et al., 2002).
evidence: This histological observation is supported by citation to Mandriota et al., 2002.

claim: The loss of pVHL is associated clinically with both the stabilization of HIF1 and the inappropriate cytoplasmic accumulation of fibronectin in the earliest lesions and cysts that appear during the RCC transformation process.
source: The loss of pVHL is associated clinically with both the stabilization of HIF1 and the inappropriate cytoplasmic accumulation of fibronectin in the earliest lesions and cysts that appear during the RCC transformation process (Mandriota et al., 2002).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citation to Mandriota et al., 2002.

claim: The P25L VHL mutation was found in conjunction with another VHL mutant P86R in a patient diagnosed with VHL disease.
source: One example of this is the P25L VHL mutant. This mutation was found in conjunction with another VHL mutant P86R in a patient diagnosed with VHL disease.
evidence: This is a clinical case description.

claim: P86R has been identified as a disease-causing mutation, suggesting P25L is a rare polymorphic allele of VHL rather than a disease-causing mutation.
source: P86R has been identified as a disease-causing mutation, suggesting P25L is a rare polymorphic allele of VHL rather than a disease-causing mutation (Rothberg et al., 2001).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citation to Rothberg et al., 2001.

claim: F374Y (rs150797491), M538I (rs61757375), and T519M (rs377001303) HIF2α mutations present as rare SNPs.
source: Although most reported HIF2α mutations cluster around the C-terminal hydroxylation site, P531, a handful impact residues with no clear role in HIFα regulation. Although it is tempting to speculate about new modes of HIF regulation, most of these mutations present as rare SNPs, including F374Y (rs150797491), M538I (rs61757375), and T519M (rs377001303).
evidence: This genetic observation includes SNP identifiers.

claim: By comparing the frequency of the F374Y allele in cohorts with and without PPGL, a lifetime penetrance of only 5% was predicted.
source: Indeed, by comparing the frequency of the previously mentioned F374 allele in cohorts with and without PPGL, a lifetime penetrance of only 5% was predicted (Dwight et al., 2021).
evidence: This statistical analysis is supported by citation to Dwight et al., 2021.

claim: In familial cases, the F374Y mutation is uncoupled from the PPGL phenotype.
source: This is consistent with the observation that in familial cases, the F374Y mutation is uncoupled from the PPGL phenotype (Lorenzo et al., 2013).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citation to Lorenzo et al., 2013.

claim: Hypoxemia associated with living at altitude or a chronic health condition like cyanotic heart disease is a known risk factor for developing a carotid body paraganglioma.
source: Generally, hypoxemia associated with living at altitude or a chronic health condition like cyanotic heart disease is a known risk factor for developing a carotid body paraganglioma (Lack, 1977; Lack, 1978; Arias-Stella and Valcarcel, 1976; Heath et al., 1970).
evidence: This clinical association is supported by citations to Lack, 1977; Lack, 1978; Arias-Stella and Valcarcel, 1976; Heath et al., 1970.

claim: Patients with germline mutations in SDHD are more likely to present with multiple PPGL tumors if they live at altitude than patients living at sea level.
source: Further, it has been reported that patients with germline mutations in SDHD, the gene encoding succinate dehydrogenase subunit D, are more likely to present with multiple PPGL tumors if they live at altitude than patients living at sea level (Astrom et al., 2003).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citation to Astrom et al., 2003.

claim: The HIF2α D539N mutation has been reported in patients with both PPGL and polycythemia (Class 1 phenotype) and patients with only polycythemia (Class 2 phenotype).
source: Recently, the HIF2α D539N mutation has been reported in patients with both PPGL and polycythemia (i.e. Class 1 phenotype) and patients with only polycythemia (i.e. Class 2 phenotype), suggesting that this mutation can cause either Class 1 and 2 HIF2-driven disease in different individuals (Oliveira et al., 2018; Pacak et al., 2014; Pang et al., 2019).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to Oliveira et al., 2018; Pacak et al., 2014; Pang et al., 2019.

claim: Belzutifan received approval in the US for treatment of RCC, hemangioblastoma, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (pNET) associated with VHL disease following a successful phase 3 clinical trial.
source: Recently, Belzutifan received approval in the US for treatment of RCC, hemangioblastoma, and pancreatic neuroendrocrine tumors (pNET) associated with VHL disease following a successful phase 3 clinical trial (Fallah et al., 2022).
evidence: This regulatory and clinical trial information is supported by citation to Fallah et al., 2022.

claim: A single-patient clinical trial of a patient with Pacak-Zhuang syndrome revealed that Belzutifan treatment can result in the shrinkage of paraganglioma tumors and the resolution of polycythemia.
source: but a single-patient clinical trial of a patient with Pacak-Zhuang syndrome (another name for Class 1a/b HIF2-driven disease) revealed that Belzutifan treatment can result in the shrinkage of paraganglioma tumors and the resolution of polycythemia (Kamihara et al., 2021).
evidence: This clinical case is supported by citation to Kamihara et al., 2021.

claim: The VHL disease-phenotypic spectrum could be explained solely by the varied disruption of HIFα signaling upon the loss or mutation in pVHL.
source: Here, we examine the current literature including the other emergent pseudohypoxic diseases and propose that the VHL disease-phenotypic spectrum could be explained solely by the varied disruption of HIFα signaling upon the loss or mutation in pVHL.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis proposed by the authors based on inference from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The complexities of VHL disease can be explained solely within the context of HIF dysregulation.
source: Despite a myriad of suggested HIF-independent functions for pVHL, we propose that the complexities of VHL disease can be explained solely within the context of HIF dysregulation.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis proposed by the authors based on inference from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: A gradient can be observed in which mutations that most stabilize HIF induce the most severe phenotypes.
source: A gradient can be observed in which mutations that most stabilize HIF induce the most severe phenotypes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors supported by Figure 2 and inferred from clinical and biochemical data.

claim: A complex molecular interplay between HIF1α and HIF2α is likely required for the development of RCC.
source: A complex molecular interplay between HIF1α and HIF2α is likely required for the development of RCC, which in turn can explain some puzzling aspects of VHL disease.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on inference from experimental data.

claim: HIF1α first acts as an oncogene and tumor initiator but following a switch in HIF expression, it acts as a tumor suppressor, preventing disease progression in RCC.
source: It is possible therefore, HIF1α first acts as an oncogene and tumor initiator but following a switch in HIF expression, it acts as a tumor suppressor, preventing disease progression.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on inference from experimental and clinical data.

claim: The transformation process in RCC can be driven by the coupled, perhaps interlinked, regulation of HIF1α and HIF2α.
source: Other functions of pVHL may indeed play a role and impact cellular phenotypes, but the transformation process itself can be driven by the coupled, perhaps interlinked, regulation of HIF1α and HIF2α.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on inference from experimental data.

claim: VHLΔ/ΔHIF1αΔ/Δ mice showed a drastic reduction in tumor frequency relative to VHLΔ/Δ mice.
source: VHLΔ/ΔHIF1αΔ/Δ mice (Note: all mice in the study were also Trp53 Δ/ΔRb1Δ/Δ) showed a drastic reduction in tumor frequency relative to VHLΔ/Δ mice.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a mouse model study.

claim: VHLΔ/ΔHIF2αΔ/Δ mice had only a moderate reduction in tumor frequency relative to VHLΔ/Δ mice.
source: VHLΔ/ΔHIF2αΔ/Δ mice by comparison only had a moderate reduction in tumor frequency relative to VHLΔ/Δ mice (Hoefflin et al., 2020).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citation to Hoefflin et al., 2020.

claim: The stabilization of both HIF1α and HIF2α in VHLΔ/Δ mice promotes the clear cell phenotype of tumor cells.
source: It was also observed that the stabilization of both HIF1α and HIF2α in VHLΔ/Δ mice promotes the clear cell phenotype of tumor cells while tumor cells from VHLΔ/ΔHIF1αΔ/Δ mice and VHLΔ/ΔHIF2αΔ/Δ mice had reduced frequency of the clear cell phenotype (Hoefflin et al., 2020).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citation to Hoefflin et al., 2020.

claim: Tumor cells from VHLΔ/ΔHIF1αΔ/Δ mice and VHLΔ/ΔHIF2αΔ/Δ mice had reduced frequency of the clear cell phenotype.
source: It was also observed that the stabilization of both HIF1α and HIF2α in VHLΔ/Δ mice promotes the clear cell phenotype of tumor cells while tumor cells from VHLΔ/ΔHIF1αΔ/Δ mice and VHLΔ/ΔHIF2αΔ/Δ mice had reduced frequency of the clear cell phenotype (Hoefflin et al., 2020).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citation to Hoefflin et al., 2020.

claim: The inactivation of PHD2 in the Type 1 cells of carotid body resulted in the formation of paraganglioma in mice.
source: One exception is the work of the Bishop group where the inactivation of PHD2 in the Type 1 cells of carotid body resulted in the formation of paraganglioma (Fielding et al., 2018).
evidence: This experimental observation is supported by citation to Fielding et al., 2018.
